sources.entry: bloglite - Micro-blog tool offering built-in syntax highlighting, mobile publishing and more (alternative to Twitter, Bluesky). MIT Docker

summary.one_liner: bloglite is a self-hosted micro-blogging service, similar to Twitter/Bluesky, where you write Markdown posts in a web interface.
summary.what_it_does: The README describes a Twitter/Bluesky-style micro-blogging server that you run yourself, with posts written in Markdown. It includes built-in syntax highlighting and display of LaTeX math expressions. You can publish and edit from desktop or mobile, and upload files and images to embed in posts. Posts can be found later with the built-in search. The site can automatically back up to plain text files, using a provided shell script run from a scheduled GitHub Actions workflow or Forgejo, triggered by environment variables. Installation is documented as a Docker Compose service with a SQLite database stored in a mounted volume.
use_cases: publish quick notes and links from phone or desktop
save and later search bookmarked snippets or recipes
share canned answers with students via a link
back up a blog to plain text files in git
how_to_run: Create a BLOGLITE_PASSWORD.env file containing BLOGLITE_PASSWORD
Create a docker-compose.yml using image zot.huijzer.xyz/bloglite:3 with BLOGLITE_USERNAME and BLOGLITE_DOMAIN set
Map port 3000:3000 and mount ./data:/data for the SQLite database
Optionally set BLOGLITE_TRIGGER_* variables to trigger backups on change
See bloglite/src/lib.rs for the full list of BLOGLITE_ environment variables
notable: Micro-blog layout with Markdown posts, built-in syntax highlighting and LaTeX math
Uses a small memory footprint (README says only a few MB of memory)
Automatic plain-text backup via shell script and scheduled GitHub Actions or Forgejo workflow
Posts get descriptive slug URLs for sharing
caveats: Health check is not acted on by Docker Compose; restarts need a custom script or autoheal
Backup triggering on each change requires a GitHub token or Forgejo token setup
Full environment variable list lives in source code rather than the README
